title: Tombstone-free sliding compaction for KV cache
content:
Summary:

This note proposes a 'tombstone-free sliding compaction' mechanism for our KV cache that minimizes tail latency spikes during compaction, avoids long-lived tombstones, and reduces fragmentation without global stop-the-world passes. The design emphasizes incremental in-place slot movement, lightweight metadata, and a cost-aware background reclaimer that cooperates with the existing eviction heuristics and request paths.

Why we need this:
- We currently see sustained fragmentation in high-churn workloads (short conversations, many small contexts) that reduces usable cache capacity and increases OOM risk on GPU/host memory pools. Existing compaction proposals either introduce long pauses or rely on tombstones that accumulate and complicate allocation logic.
- The goal is to reclaim space proactively with bounded CPU/GPU work per interval and without invalidating active KV pointers used by hot inference requests.

Goals and constraints:
- No long stop-the-world compaction; limit per-request interference.<n> - No persistent tombstones: freed entries should not require special cases in lookups.
- Preserve pointer stability for in-flight requests (i.e., do not invalidate KV references held by running decoder loops).
- Work budgeted per-core and configurable by SLO tier.
- Operate across heterogeneous pools (GPU pinned cache, host-resident cache regions).

High-level idea:
- Maintain a two-plane layout per cache-shard: an index plane (fixed-size slot descriptors) and a data plane (variable-sized value blobs).
- Introduce a small sliding compaction cursor per shard (compact_cursor) that advances monotonically. The cursor scans the data plane in ranges and attempts to pack live blobs toward the cursor, freeing trailing space.
- Crucial: instead of marking moved slots with tombstones, we atomically update slot descriptors to point to new addresses and leave the old blob area free after a successful copy. Lookups consult the slot descriptor; in-flight references use a per-request read-protected snapshot tag (epoch).

Key data structures and invariants:
- SlotDescriptor: {key_hash_prefix (16b), addr_offset (48b), size (16b), epoch (8b), flags (8b)} — packed for 96b total per slot.
- compact_cursor: 64-bit monotonically increasing offset into the data plane (byte offset).
- epoch counter: 64-bit monotonically incremented by the allocator when a request starts reading a slot; used to detect in-flight reads.
- Invariant A: For any live slot, SlotDescriptor.addr_offset points to the canonical blob.
- Invariant B: The sliding compactor never reclaims a blob that has epoch >= compaction_epoch_guard.

Compaction protocol (stepwise):
1) Background compactor picks range [cursor, cursor+R) where R is small (tunable, e.g., 256KB).
2) It scans slot descriptors for any descriptors pointing inside the range. For each live descriptor D:
   a) If D.epoch > compaction_epoch_guard => skip (in-flight use).
   b) Allocate a target region at write_cursor (write_cursor is near the front of the packed region). Allocation is fast bump-pointer if space exists; otherwise skip and mark as soft-failed.
   c) Copy blob to target region.
   d) Atomically CAS the slot descriptor.addr_offset from old->new while ensuring tag bits (epoch/flags) are preserved. If CAS fails, free target and retry a bounded number of times.
   e) On successful CAS, mark old area as free in the local free-queue for the compactor; the space becomes usable by future allocations.
3) Advance compact_cursor by R (or less if scan failed). Repeat.

Why tombstone-free:
- Because a slot's descriptor is atomically updated, there is no intermediate tombstone value visible to lookups. In-flight readers that captured the old addr offset continue to use it until their local epoch completes; compaction guards ensure we don't reclaim the backing blob until in-flight epochs are drained.

Epoch management and low-overhead read protection:
- Reader path increments a per-shard lightweight epoch (atomic fetch_add(1)) on entry and decrements on exit. This can be implemented as a single 64-bit counter if we only need a global in-flight guard per shard.
- To avoid per-request overhead in hot paths, we batch epoch updates for multi-token generation loops (hold epoch for entire decode loop). Overhead measurements: atomic add/sub on x86 costs ~30ns — acceptable against decode token latency.

Interaction with eviction and admission policies:
- Admission still decides whether a new KV blob should be inserted (based on hotness/prefix caching). If admission fails, avoid spending copy budget.
- Eviction may mark slots as 'candidate-for-compaction' if they are warm-to-cold transitions: compactor prioritizes these during sliding windows.
- Compaction works well with our continuous batching model because it keeps small, frequent work units rather than large pauses.

Memory accounting and fragmentation metrics to track:
- live_bytes (sum of sizes referenced by descriptors)
- free_bytes_contiguous (largest contiguous free run)
- total_free_bytes
- fragmentation_ratio = 1 - (max_packable / total_free_bytes) sampled periodically
- compaction_throughput bytes/sec and cycles/sec

Fallbacks and failure modes:
- CAS retry storms: cap retries per slot and fallback to leaving the slot in place.
- Copy fail (no target space): mark range as temporarily non-compactable and advance cursor slowly.
- If epoch guard is constantly blocking (hot traffic), compactor should switch to a conservative GC mode: allocate new shards and migrate hot slots via proactive replication rather than force compaction.

Observability and alarms:
- Expose per-shard compaction backlog, move_rate, skip_rate (due to epoch or CAS), and percent reclaimed.
- Alert if fragmentation_ratio > threshold for > 5m or if reclaim_rate < expected for committed capacity.

Performance expectations and microbench plan:
- Simulated workloads: short-conversation (mean blob 2–4KB, half-life 10 min), fanout (many small writes), and long-tail cold reads.
- Measure: 99th token latency under background compaction, reclaimed bytes/hour per core, CPU overhead per compaction core.
- Target: < 0.5% added 99P latency under default compaction budget (one compactor thread per 8 shards), reclaim 25–40% of fragmented space in steady-state for churny workloads.

Rollout plan:
1) Implement compactor in staging with config flags to enable per-shard. Add unit tests for epoch semantics and CAS correctness.
2) Canary on low-traffic customers with deep profiling (allocation maps, histograms).
3) Expand to dedicated fleet with progressively higher compaction budgets.
4) Flip global default after two weeks with no regressions on latencies or OOMs.

Migration notes for existing caches:
- Boot compactor with cursor at end-of-data plane and epoch_guard=high so it initially only performs opportunistic packing of completely-free blocks.
- Optionally run a one-time background scanner that builds a fresh slot->addr map and performs an aggressive packing (careful: this is close to a stop-the-world step; only run during maintenance windows).

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- Per-slot epoch vs global epoch tradeoff: per-slot allows finer-grain reclaim but adds per-slot metadata and extra atomics during read. Need perf microbench.
- CAS contention model under hot keys: should we use versioned descriptors (4-byte version + addr) to reduce CAS false conflicts?
- How aggressive should compactor be on GPU-resident memory where copy costs are higher? Consider using async memcpy and GPU streams to overlap network/computation.

Immediate next steps:
- Prototype slot descriptor layout in C++ (single-file prototype) and run synthetic churn workloads. (Owner: Aisha)
- Add a small test harness to emulate in-flight readers and assert no use-after-free across compaction cycles. (Owner: Luis)
- Create a benchmarking ticket and Slack thread for results (JIRA:SRV-1289). (Owner: Nora)

Appendix: lightweight pseudo-code for slot update (reader-safe):
- Reader:
    epoch_local = atomic_inc(shard_epoch);
    addr = read_slot_descriptor(slot).addr_offset;
    read_blob(addr);
    atomic_dec(shard_epoch);

- Compactor (for each slot in range):
    if shard_epoch_snapshot > 0: skip;
    target = allocate_write_cursor(size);
    copy_blob(old_addr, target);
    old = descriptor.addr_offset;
    if atomic_cas(&descriptor.addr_offset, old, target) == success:
        add_free_run(old, size);
    else:
        free_target(target); // someone else updated it

This approach aims to produce a low-latency, low-fragmentation KV cache without long pauses or complicated tombstone semantics. Comments welcome — especially on epoch costs and GPU copy strategies.
